import sys

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    if not data:
        return
    pos = 0
    W = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    T = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    taps = [int(data[pos + i]) for i in range(T)]; pos += T
    seed = int(data[pos]); pos += 1
    cycles = int(data[pos]); pos += 1

    mask = (1 << W) - 1
    reg = seed & mask
    start = reg

    values = []
    bits = []
    period = None

    for c in range(1, cycles + 1):
        fb = 0
        for t in taps:
            fb ^= (reg >> t) & 1
        out_bit = (reg >> (W - 1)) & 1
        reg = ((reg << 1) | fb) & mask
        values.append(reg)
        bits.append(out_bit)
        if period is None and reg == start:
            period = c

    print("values%s" % "".join(" %d" % v for v in values))
    print("bits%s" % "".join(" %d" % b for b in bits))
    print("period %s" % ("none" if period is None else period))

main()

explanation:
## One cycle

```cpp
unsigned fb{ 0 };
for (int t : taps) fb ^= (reg >> t) & 1u;
unsigned outBit{ (reg >> (W - 1)) & 1u };

reg = ((reg << 1) | fb) & mask;
```

Three reads of `reg`, then one write. The write is last, and that ordering is
the entire correctness argument.

`(reg >> t) & 1` is the standard "give me bit t" idiom: shift it down to position
0, then mask off everything above. `fb` starting at 0 is also the identity for
XOR, which is why a tap list of length 0 gives a feedback of 0 with no special
case - the XOR of nothing is 0, just as the sum of nothing is 0.

## Read everything, then write once

The hardware is a row of flip-flops sharing one clock:

```
        +---+     +---+     +---+     +---+
 fb --->| 0 |---->| 1 |---->| 2 |---->| 3 |---> outBit
        +---+     +---+     +---+     +---+
          ^                   |         |
          |                   |         |
          +--------- XOR <----+---------+
                         taps 2 and 3
```

At the clock edge, every flip-flop captures what its input *was* just before the
edge. The XOR gate is combinational and its inputs are the old outputs of
flip-flops 2 and 3. So all four bits update simultaneously from the old state -
there is no sequence, no "first this one then that one".

Writing it with the assignment last reproduces that. The broken version does
not:

```cpp
reg = (reg << 1) & mask;                       // shifted already
unsigned fb = ((reg >> 3) & 1) ^ ((reg >> 2) & 1);   // reads the NEW bits
reg |= fb;
```

That computes the feedback from bits that have already moved, which is a
different machine with a different sequence. It will produce plausible-looking
pseudo-random output and will not match any LFSR, nor any circuit.

## This is `=` versus `<=` in Verilog

```verilog
// correct: nonblocking, all flip-flops update from the old state
always @(posedge clk)
    if (rst) reg_q <= 4'b0001;
    else     reg_q <= {reg_q[2:0], reg_q[3] ^ reg_q[2]};

// wrong: blocking, so later lines see earlier updates
always @(posedge clk) begin
    reg_q = {reg_q[2:0], 1'b0};
    reg_q[0] = reg_q[3] ^ reg_q[2];     // reads the already-shifted value
end
```

Nonblocking assignment (`<=`) evaluates every right-hand side in the whole
always block first, then commits every left-hand side. That is exactly what a
clock edge does. Blocking assignment (`=`) commits immediately, so statement
order becomes semantics - and worse, the *simulator* follows your statement
order while the *synthesiser* builds whatever gates it thinks you meant. The two
then disagree, and a design that simulates correctly fails in silicon.

Hence the rule every style guide gives: **`<=` in clocked blocks, `=` in
combinational ones.** The C++ version in this problem is the same discipline
expressed as "read all the inputs into locals, then assign".

## Why the period is 15 and not 16

Four bits have 16 states, but 0 is a fixed point - from zero the feedback is
zero and the register never leaves. So the reachable cycle has at most
`2^4 - 1 = 15` states, and a **maximal-length** tap set visits all of them.

Taps 3 and 2 on 4 bits correspond to the polynomial `x^4 + x^3 + 1`, which is
primitive over GF(2) - that is the algebraic condition for maximal length. Which
tap sets are primitive is not something you derive at the bench; you look it up.
Xilinx application note XAPP052 is the standard table, covering 3 to 168 bits,
and it famously lists 4 taps as sufficient for every width in that range.

One hidden case has a **single** tap at bit `W-1`, which makes the feedback the
bit being shifted out - so the register simply rotates, and from a seed of 1 the
period is 4 rather than 15. A non-primitive tap set does not just give a shorter
cycle; it splits the state space into several disjoint cycles of different
lengths, so the period depends on the seed as well as the taps. Another hidden
case is a 16-bit register whose full period is 65535 - far longer than the 64
cycles simulated, so its answer is `period none`. That is the honest result: the
simulation did not run long enough to see it come round, and reporting a number
would be a guess.

## Seeding, and the lock-up

```
input:  4 2 / taps 3 2 / seed 0 / 5 cycles
values 0 0 0 0 0
bits 0 0 0 0 0
period 1
```

The all-zeros state is self-sustaining, which is a property of the circuit and
not of the code. Every real design deals with it:

- **reset to a non-zero value** - the usual fix, and why you see `<= 1` in reset
  branches
- **invert the feedback** (`fb = ~XOR(...)`) to make *all-ones* the dead state
  instead, which is preferable when the register powers up at zero
- **detect and inject** - a NOR of all bits forced into the feedback, which turns
  the dead state into a 2^W-length cycle at the cost of a wide gate

`period 1` is the correct output here, because the register does return to its
seed after one cycle - it never left.

## Where LFSRs are used, and where they are not

**Used** because they are nearly free - W flip-flops and a handful of XOR gates,
one clock cycle per bit, no multiplier and no carry chain:

- **CRC** - a CRC *is* an LFSR whose input is XORed into the feedback. Ethernet,
  ZIP and PNG all use CRC-32, which is a 32-bit LFSR
- **scrambling** - PCIe, SATA and USB 3 XOR the data with an LFSR stream so the
  line has no long runs of identical bits, which keeps clock recovery working
- **built-in self test** - an LFSR generates pseudo-random stimulus and another
  compacts the responses into a signature, which is how a chip tests itself with
  almost no extra area
- **cheap counters** - an LFSR counter needs no carry propagation, so it runs at
  a higher clock than a binary counter of the same width, when you only need to
  count *to* something rather than know *where* you are

**Not** used for anything security-related. The sequence is linear, so observing
`W` consecutive output bits lets you solve for the entire state and predict
every future bit, by Gaussian elimination. The content-scrambling system on DVDs
was two LFSRs and was broken in 1999; the A5/1 cipher in GSM was three and was
broken as well. An LFSR is a *pseudo-random* generator in the statistical sense
only, and the distinction between "passes randomness tests" and
"unpredictable to an adversary" is the whole of cryptography.
